To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the estimation error covariance of a linear system using analog amplify and forward with multiple sensors decays with $1/M$ for large $M$, and that the power allocation that minimizes the estimation error covariance is the one that minimizes the variance of the sum of the received signal to interference ratios at the fusion center.
1) in many situations, state estimation error covariance decaying at a rate of 1/M can be achieved, and 2) optimal power allocation is achieved by a greedy algorithm.

(i) for large M, the error covariance decays as 1/M for many situations, (ii) optimal power allocation is achieved by a greedy algorithm, (iii) a sub-optimal estimator is derived when channel state information is unavailable.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the design of optimal state estimation algorithms for wireless sensor networks with a large number of sensors, where each sensor transmits its noisy measurement of the system state over a fading channel.
state estimation over fading channels using multiple sensors, for multiple access and orthogonal multiple access.
state estimation of linear dynamical systems using multiple sensors over wireless channels.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the optimal power allocation for the multiple access case is to use the same power for all sensors, and that the optimal power for orthogonal access is proportional to the inverse of the channel gain.

for a system of $N$ linear time invariant discrete time stochastic systems with $M$ sensors and $M$ orthogonal channels, the optimal state estimator at the fusion center can be achieved by using an adaptive Kalman filter.
in the large $M$ case the performance is dominated by the channel noise, and not by the estimation error.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown how the estimation error covariance scales with the number of sensors and the number of sensors can be allocated optimally to maximize the performance.
we have developed a framework for state estimation over wireless channels with multiple sensors, where the optimal estimation is achieved at the fusion centre using a time varying KF.
the estimation error covariance converges to zero at a rate of 1/M when the number of sensor is large, and the optimal transmission powers are linearly proportional to the channel gains.
The main takeaway from our work is that
in order for the state estimator to perform well, the sensors must be well separated in the network.
in many situations it is possible to achieve optimal state estimation using a linear estimator, and the optimal power allocations can be computed efficiently.
for a fixed number of sensors, the performance of the system improves when the number of bits transmitted per symbol increases.
